q: According to kinetic molecular theory, diffusion is much slower in liquids than in gases because liquid molecules:
o: Are close together and attract each other, with little free space to move in
Are much heavier than gas molecules
Move only in straight lines without collisions
x: Liquid molecules are always moving, but they are packed closely and held by intermolecular forces, so they collide constantly and travel only short distances. Gas molecules have large empty spaces and weak attractions, so they spread out quickly.

q: Liquids are almost incompressible because:
o: Their molecules have no kinetic energy
There is very little empty space between their molecules
Their molecules repel each other strongly at all distances
x: Liquid molecules are already very close to one another, so pressure can push them only slightly closer. Gases are easily compressed because most of their volume is empty space.

q: A liquid has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container. In terms of kinetic molecular theory, this is because its molecules:
o: Are held close by intermolecular forces but can slide past one another
Are fixed in definite positions in a lattice
Are far apart and move freely in all directions
Have no attractive forces between them
x: Intermolecular forces keep liquid molecules close, fixing the volume, but the molecules are not locked in place, so the liquid can flow and take any shape. Fixed lattice positions describe solids; free, distant molecules describe gases.

q: A drop of ink spreads faster through hot water than through cold water. This is because at higher temperature the water molecules:
o: Have greater average kinetic energy and move faster
x: Raising the temperature increases the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so they move and mix faster and diffusion speeds up. Stronger forces or tighter packing would slow diffusion, not speed it up.

q: On heating through the same temperature range, a liquid generally expands:
o: More than a solid but less than a gas
Exactly as much as a gas
x: Intermolecular forces in liquids are weaker than in solids but much stronger than in gases. So when the molecules gain energy, liquids expand more than solids and much less than gases.

q: Compared with the intermolecular forces in a gas, those in a liquid are:
x: In a liquid the molecules are close together, so intermolecular attractions are strong enough to hold them in a definite volume. In a gas the molecules are far apart and these forces are very weak.

q: According to kinetic molecular theory, the average kinetic energy of the molecules of a liquid depends on:
x: Average kinetic energy is directly proportional to absolute temperature. A larger or differently shaped sample at the same temperature has the same average kinetic energy per molecule.

q: Which is the correct order of increasing strength of intermolecular forces?
o: Hydrogen bonding < dipole–dipole forces < London dispersion forces
Dipole–dipole forces < London dispersion forces < hydrogen bonding
London dispersion forces < dipole–dipole forces < hydrogen bonding
London dispersion forces < hydrogen bonding < dipole–dipole forces
x: For molecules of similar size, London (dispersion) forces are the weakest, dipole–dipole forces are stronger, and hydrogen bonding is the strongest kind of intermolecular force.

q: In which pair of liquids are the attractions between molecules only London dispersion forces?
x: Hexane and CCl₄ are non-polar molecules (CCl₄ is symmetrical, so its bond dipoles cancel), so only London forces act. Chloroform and propanone are polar (dipole–dipole forces), and the other two pairs show hydrogen bonding.

q: Which of the following noble gases has the highest boiling point?
x: Noble gases are held only by London dispersion forces, which grow stronger as atoms get larger and more polarisable. Krypton is the largest of these four, so it has the highest boiling point.

q: Evaporation of a liquid:
o: Takes place only at the boiling point
Takes place throughout the whole body of the liquid
Takes place at all temperatures from the surface of the liquid
Takes place only in a closed container
x: Evaporation is a surface process that happens at any temperature, because some surface molecules always have enough energy to escape. Boiling, by contrast, happens throughout the liquid at one temperature for a given pressure.

q: Evaporation causes cooling of the remaining liquid because:
o: The molecules with the highest kinetic energy escape, lowering the average kinetic energy
The molecules with the lowest kinetic energy escape first
Intermolecular forces in the remaining liquid disappear
The remaining liquid absorbs energy from its vapour
x: Only the most energetic surface molecules can overcome the attractions and escape. The molecules left behind have a lower average kinetic energy, so the temperature of the liquid falls.

q: Which of the following does NOT increase the rate of evaporation of a liquid?
o: Stronger intermolecular attractions in the liquid
x: Stronger intermolecular forces make it harder for molecules to escape, so evaporation is slower. Larger surface area, higher temperature and moving air all speed up evaporation.

q: The vapour pressure of a liquid is the pressure exerted by its vapour when:
o: The vapour is in equilibrium with the liquid in a closed vessel at a given temperature
The liquid is boiling in an open vessel
x: In a closed vessel, evaporation and condensation become equal in rate (dynamic equilibrium). The pressure of the vapour at that point, at a given temperature, is the vapour pressure.

q: The vapour pressure of a pure liquid in a closed vessel depends on:
o: The temperature and the nature of the liquid
The surface area of the liquid
x: Vapour pressure is set by the temperature and by the strength of intermolecular forces in that liquid. Changing the amount of liquid, its surface area or the vessel volume changes how fast equilibrium is reached, not the equilibrium vapour pressure.

q: The boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which:
o: Its vapour pressure becomes equal to the external pressure
Its density is at a maximum
x: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the pressure above it; bubbles of vapour can then form throughout the liquid. Evaporation happens at all temperatures, so it does not mark the boiling point.

q: Water boils below 100 °C on a high mountain such as Murree because:
o: The atmospheric pressure is lower there
The water has more dissolved salts
The intermolecular forces in water become stronger
x: At high altitude the external pressure is less than 1 atm, so water's vapour pressure reaches it at a lower temperature. A boiling point depends on external pressure, not on air temperature.

q: Food cooks faster in a pressure cooker because:
o: The higher pressure lowers the boiling point of water
Steam has a lower temperature than boiling water
The pressure breaks the hydrogen bonds in water
The higher pressure raises the boiling point of water
x: Inside the sealed cooker the pressure is above 1 atm, so water boils at a temperature above 100 °C. The hotter water cooks food faster.

q: At the same temperature (20 °C), which liquid has the highest vapour pressure?
x: Diethyl ether has no O–H group and cannot hydrogen bond with itself, so its molecules escape most easily. Ethanol, water and glycerol all hydrogen bond, and glycerol, with three O–H groups, has the lowest vapour pressure.

q: At 1 atm, liquid X boils at a higher temperature than liquid Y. At the same temperature, compared with Y, liquid X has:
o: Higher vapour pressure and stronger intermolecular forces
Lower vapour pressure and weaker intermolecular forces
Lower vapour pressure and stronger intermolecular forces
Higher vapour pressure and weaker intermolecular forces
x: A higher boiling point means X must be heated more to raise its vapour pressure to 1 atm, so at any given temperature its vapour pressure is lower. This happens because its molecules attract each other more strongly.

q: Some liquids that decompose at their normal boiling point are purified by vacuum distillation. This works because:
o: Lowering the external pressure raises the boiling point
Lowering the external pressure lowers the boiling point
A vacuum increases the intermolecular forces
A vacuum stops evaporation from the surface
x: Under reduced pressure, the liquid's vapour pressure equals the external pressure at a lower temperature, so it boils below its decomposition temperature. This is the same reason water boils below 100 °C at high altitude.

q: A hydrogen bond is an attraction between:
o: A hydrogen atom bonded to F, O or N and a lone pair on another F, O or N atom
Two hydrogen atoms in an H₂ molecule
A hydrogen ion and a metal atom
A hydrogen atom and any carbon atom
x: When hydrogen is bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom (F, O or N), it becomes partly positive and is attracted to a lone pair on a nearby electronegative atom. The H–H bond in H₂ is an ordinary covalent bond.

q: Which of the following does NOT show hydrogen bonding between its own molecules?
x: Sulphur is larger and much less electronegative than O, N or F, so H₂S does not form hydrogen bonds. H₂O, NH₃ and HF are the classic examples of hydrogen-bonded liquids.

q: Which shows the correct order of boiling points?
x: Water boils at 100 °C, HF at about 20 °C and NH₃ at about −33 °C. Water is highest because each molecule takes part in more hydrogen bonds; NH₃ is lowest because N is the least electronegative of the three.

q: Fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen, yet water boils at a higher temperature than HF. The reason is that:
o: Each water molecule can form more hydrogen bonds on average, having two H atoms and two lone pairs
The hydrogen bonds in water are individually stronger than those in HF
Water molecules are heavier than HF molecules
HF does not form hydrogen bonds
x: HF has only one H atom per molecule, so it forms on average one hydrogen bond per molecule (chains). Water, with two H atoms and two lone pairs, forms on average two per molecule, giving a 3-D network that needs more energy to break.

q: In solid and liquid hydrogen fluoride, the molecules are linked by hydrogen bonds into:
o: Flat hexagonal rings of six molecules
x: Each HF molecule has only one hydrogen atom, so the molecules join end to end through F–H···F hydrogen bonds into zig-zag chains. The 3-D tetrahedral network is the structure of ice.

q: Water (H₂O, 18 g mol⁻¹) is a liquid at room temperature, but hydrogen sulphide (H₂S, 34 g mol⁻¹) is a gas. This is because:
o: Water molecules are linked by hydrogen bonds
x: Although H₂S is heavier, it cannot hydrogen bond, while water molecules are held by strong hydrogen bonds that need much more energy to separate. Without hydrogen bonding, water would be expected to boil below H₂S.

q: Ammonia is very soluble in water mainly because:
o: Ammonia and water have the same molar mass
Ammonia reacts with water to form hydrogen gas
Ammonia molecules form hydrogen bonds with water molecules
x: The N–H hydrogens of NH₃ bond to oxygen lone pairs in water, and water's O–H hydrogens bond to the lone pair on nitrogen. These hydrogen bonds make NH₃ highly soluble. NH₃ is polar, not non-polar.

q: In ice, the maximum number of hydrogen bonds in which a single water molecule takes part is:
x: Each water molecule forms two hydrogen bonds through its two H atoms and accepts two more at its two lone pairs, so it is linked to four neighbours arranged tetrahedrally.

q: Compared with the covalent O–H bond inside a water molecule, a hydrogen bond between water molecules is:
x: A hydrogen bond is an intermolecular attraction and is much weaker than a covalent bond, although it is the strongest kind of intermolecular force. This is why boiling water separates molecules without breaking O–H bonds.

q: Considered as a single bond, which hydrogen bond is the strongest?
x: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, so the F–H bond is most polar and F–H···F is the strongest single hydrogen bond. N–H···N is weaker than O–H···O, and S–H···S is hardly a hydrogen bond at all.

q: Water has its maximum density at:
x: Liquid water is densest at 4 °C. Below this temperature it expands again as molecules start arranging into the open, hydrogen-bonded structure of ice.

q: At 0 °C, the density of ice is about:
x: Ice (about 0.92 g cm⁻³) is roughly 9% less dense than liquid water (about 1.00 g cm⁻³), because hydrogen bonds hold its molecules in an open lattice. That is why about nine-tenths of an iceberg lies under water.

q: When a fixed mass of water is warmed from 0 °C to 4 °C, its volume:
x: Between 0 °C and 4 °C, remaining open hydrogen-bonded clusters collapse and molecules move closer, so the volume falls and the density rises to its maximum at 4 °C. Above 4 °C water expands normally.

q: When water is cooled from 10 °C to 0 °C, its density:
x: Water contracts as it cools down to 4 °C, so its density rises; below 4 °C it expands, so the density falls again. This is the anomalous behaviour of water.

q: Fish can survive in a lake in winter even when the surface is frozen because:
o: Ice forms on top and insulates the liquid water below it
The whole lake freezes, but fish do not need water
Ice is denser and sinks, leaving warm water at the top
Water below 4 °C sinks to the bottom
x: Water at 4 °C is densest and sinks; colder water and then ice stay on top. The floating ice layer insulates the water below, which stays liquid. Water colder than 4 °C rises, it does not sink.

q: In ice, each oxygen atom is surrounded by four other oxygen atoms linked through hydrogen bonds, arranged:
o: In closely packed layers with no spaces
Tetrahedrally, forming an open cage-like structure
x: Two hydrogen bonds are formed through the H atoms and two through the lone pairs, so the four neighbours are arranged tetrahedrally. This gives an open structure with empty spaces, which is why ice is less dense than water.

q: When ice melts at 0 °C to give water at 0 °C, the volume:
o: Increases, because the molecules gain kinetic energy
Increases, because hydrogen bonds become stronger
Decreases, because the open hydrogen-bonded structure partly collapses
x: On melting, some hydrogen bonds break and the open cage collapses, so molecules fill some of the empty spaces and pack more closely. The water therefore occupies less volume than the ice it came from.

q: In a deep lake whose surface has frozen in winter, the water at the bottom is at about:
x: Water at 4 °C has the highest density, so it sinks and collects at the bottom, while colder, less dense water stays near the surface and freezes at 0 °C.

q: Water pipes sometimes burst on very cold nights because:
o: Ice contracts and pulls the pipe apart
Water contracts as it cools below 4 °C
Water expands when it freezes into ice
x: When water freezes, the molecules lock into the open hydrogen-bonded structure of ice, which takes more volume than the liquid. This expansion can crack pipes. Below 4 °C water expands, it does not contract.

q: A sample of liquid water is at exactly 4 °C. If it is warmed by 2 °C, or instead cooled by 2 °C, its volume will:
o: Increase on warming and decrease on cooling
Decrease on warming and increase on cooling
x: At 4 °C water has its maximum density and so its minimum volume. Any change of temperature from 4 °C, up or down, lowers the density and therefore increases the volume.
